fetched_contents.text: Efficacy and Safety of Fenfluramine in Epilepsy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Abstract Introduction Fenfluramine (FFA) is an amphetamine derivative that promotes the release and blocks the neuronal reuptake of serotonin. Initially introduced as an appetite suppressant, FFA also showed antiseizure properties. This systematic review aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of FFA for the treatment of seizures in patients with epilepsy. Methods We systematically searched (in week 3 of June 2022) MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and the US National Institutes of Health Clinical Trials Registry. Randomized, double- or single-blinded, placebo-controlled studies of FFA in patients with epilepsy and uncontrolled seizures were identified. Efficacy outcomes included the proportions of patients with ≥ 50% and 100% reductions in baseline seizure frequency during the treatment period. Tolerability outcomes included the proportions of patients who withdrew from treatment for any reason and suffered adverse events (AEs). The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed according to the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. The risk ratio (RR) along with the 95% confidence interval (CI) were estimated for each outcome. Results Three trials were identified and a total of 469 Dravet syndrome (DS) and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (LGS) subjects were randomized. All three trials were judged to be at low risk of biases. In patients with DS, the RRs for ≥ 50% and 100% reductions in convulsive seizure frequency for the FFA group compared to placebo were 5.61 (95% CI 2.73–11.54) and 4.71 (95% CI 0.57–39.30), respectively. In patients with LGS, the corresponding RRs for ≥ 50% and 100% reductions in drop seizure frequency were 2.58 (95% CI 1.33–5.02) and 0.50 (95% CI 0.031–7.81), respectively. The drug was withdrawn for any reason in 10.1% and 5.8% of patients receiving FFA and placebo, respectively (RR 1.79, 95% CI 0.89–3.59). Treatment discontinuation due to AEs occurred in 5.4% and 1.2% of FFA- and placebo-treated patients, respectively (RR 3.63, 95% CI 0.93–14.16). Decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue, and weight loss were AEs associated with FFA treatment. Conclusion Fenfluramine reduces the frequency of seizures in patients with DS and LGS. Decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue, and weight loss are non-cardiovascular AEs associated with FFA. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40120-023-00452-1. Keywords: Epilepsy, Seizures, Dravet syndrome, Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, Fenfluramine Key Summary Points Adjunctive fenfluramine (FFA) reduces the frequency of convulsive seizures in patients with Dravet syndrome. Adjunctive FFA reduces the frequency of drop seizures in patients with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. Non-cardiovascular adverse events associated with FFA include decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue, and weight loss. Introduction Epilepsy is one of the most common chronic disorders of the brain. The management is mainly symptomatic, and most patients reach sustained freedom from seizures. Around one-third of people with epilepsy, however, continue to experience seizures despite adequate treatment [1, 2]. Uncontrolled epilepsy is often disabling and associated with significant psychological and social dysfunction, impaired quality of life, and risk of premature death [3]. There remains, hence, the urgent need to search for new therapeutic options. Fenfluramine (3-trifluoromethyl-N-ethylamphetamine) (FFA) has a long-standing history. The drug was introduced in the early 1960s as an appetite suppressant with less stimulating side effects than existing amphetamines. The anorectic effect was thought to be mediated by serotonergic mechanisms, as FFA both promotes the release of serotonin (5-HT) and blocks its neuronal reuptake [4, 5]. The drug was approved for the short-term treatment of obesity, but safety concerns arose in the 1980s when its use was associated with the occurrence of pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease in some individuals given up to 220 mg per day [6, 7]. The medication was, hence, withdrawn from the US market in 1997. The antiseizure effects of FFA were first described in the 1980s by Aicardi and Gastaut in three adolescent patients with intractable self-induced photosensitive epilepsy [8] and later reported in small case series and observational studies of children with intractable and self-induced epilepsy [9]. In 2002, a Belgian Royal Decree was issued to grant compassionate use approval of FFA in paediatric patients with intractable epilepsy and to allow patients with Dravet syndrome (DS) to be treated under a treatment protocol [10]. Some of these patients with DS have been given FFA for up to 30 years with reductions in seizure frequency and no evidence of cardiopulmonary disease [10–12]; the mean doses reported in the two cohorts of Belgian patients were 0.27 mg/kg and 0.35 mg/kg per day [13]. In 2020, FFA was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of seizures associated with DS in patients aged 2 years and older, and by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of seizures associated with DS as an add-on therapy to other anti-epileptic medicines for patients 2 years of age and older. In March 2022, the FDA approved the use of FFA for the treatment of seizures associated with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (LGS) in patients 2 years of age and older. In December 2022, the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use of the EMA adopted a new indication for FFA as an add-on therapy for seizures associated with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome for patients aged 2 years and older. This study systematically evaluated and synthesized the evidence about the efficacy and safety of FFA as a treatment for seizures in patients with epilepsy. fetched_contents.text: Fenfluramine treatment in pediatric patients with Dravet syndrome reduces seizure burden and overall healthcare costs: A retrospective and observational real‐world study Abstract Objectives Dravet syndrome is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by early onset epilepsy with multiple seizure types often intractable to treatment. Randomized clinical trials have demonstrated how treatment with fenfluramine significantly reduces seizure frequency in patients with Dravet syndrome. The study aims to (1) describe the efficacy and tolerability of fenfluramine in a Danish cohort of patients with Dravet syndrome; and (2) evaluate whether treatment with fenfluramine reduces epilepsy‐related hospital contacts administrated by pediatricians or epilepsy‐trained nurses. Methods A retrospective registry‐based cohort study at the Danish Epilepsy Centre, Filadelfia, Dianalund, Denmark, enrolled 30 pediatric patients with Dravet syndrome treated with fenfluramine between 2017 and 2023. Results Thirty patients with Dravet syndrome (aged 3–21 years, 12 females) with a verified pathogenic SCN1A variant were included. They were treated with fenfluramine at a mean duration of 29 months with a mean maintenance dose of 0.5 mg/kg/day. The number of patient‐years on treatment was 75 years. At last follow‐up, 6 patients had discontinued treatment due to lack of efficacy or adverse effects. In the remaining 24 patients, generalized tonic–clonic seizures were reduced by ≥30% in 83%, by ≥50% in 67%, and by 100% in 25%. Additionally, 71% of the patients were reduced in concomitant anti‐seizure medication, and 75% experienced a reduction (mean reduction at 52%, range 11%–94%) in epilepsy‐related hospital contacts from baseline to the end of the treatment period. Significance Treatment with fenfluramine effectively reduced seizure frequency and concomitant antiseizure medication in patients with Dravet syndrome. Furthermore, a decrease in epilepsy‐related contacts by 80% was observed over 6 years of treatment, which may indicate cost‐effective benefits. Plain Language Summary Patients with Dravet syndrome suffer from severe epileptic seizures that are difficult to treat with medication. Earlier, treatment with fenfluramine (an anti‐seizure medication) has been documented to decrease the total number of seizures in patients with Dravet syndrome. This publication summarizes the experiences with fenfluramine in children with Dravet syndrome at the Danish Epilepsy Centre, Filadelfia, Dianalund, Denmark. Our publication also illustrates that treatment with fenfluramine may reduce the patients' number of yearly contacts with doctors and nurses specialized in epilepsy treatment, which may indicate cost‐effectiveness. INTRODUCTION Fenfluramine was initially marketed as an appetite suppressant but withdrawn from the market in 1997 due to associations with cardiac valvulopathy. 1 , 2 Based on the results of three phase 3, placebo‐controlled randomized clinical trials (RCTs), demonstrating significantly reduced frequency of major motor seizures in patients with Dravet syndrome (DS), fenfluramine was approved as a repurposed drug for the treatment of DS in 2020. 3 , 4 , 5 Fenfluramine is thought to enhance serotonin (5‐HT) release and serotonergic signaling via different 5‐HT receptors (5‐HT1D and 5‐HT2A and 2c) and acts as a positive modulator of sigma‐1 opioid receptors. 6 , 7 This will probably affect seizure activity and GABAergic neurotransmission. However, the exact mechanism of action that leads to seizure prevention in patients with DS is not fully clarified. DS is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by early onset intractable epilepsy with multiple seizure types often triggered by elevated body temperature, intellectual disability, behavioral problems, psychiatric comorbidities, and progressive gait impairments. 8 , 9 , 10 DS is primarily caused by loss‐of‐function variants in SCN1A, encoding the alpha subunit of the voltage‐gated sodium channel, type 1 (Nav1.1). 11 Seizures associated with fever begin in the first year of life with subsequent development of afebrile seizure types. The majority of patients with DS experience episodes of status epilepticus; in addition sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) is the main cause of premature mortality. 8 , 10 In the Nordic countries, valproic acid is listed as the first‐line treatment for children with DS, while add‐on treatment with stiripentol and clobazam is the second‐line treatment. 8 , 12 The treatments used for DS are intended to reduce the seizure burden, and since the majority of patients with DS continue to have poorly controlled seizures, new therapeutic options are necessary. 13 In international expertise groups, fenfluramine has therefore been suggested as a new second‐line treatment option. 10 However, data describing the use of fenfluramine in the treatment of seizures in DS in real‐world settings are limited 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 and no “real‐life data” from the treatment of DS with fenfluramine in the Nordic Countries has been reported. Methods Patients with DS were treated with fenfluramine in the European Union Early Access Program (EAP). Following a 28‐day baseline period to establish the pretreatment monthly convulsive seizure frequency (MCSF), fenfluramine was started at a dose chosen by the treating physician and gradually titrated based on efficacy and tolerability up to a maximum of 0.7 mg/kg/day. Seizure incidence was recorded in a written diary, and adverse events (AEs) were reported at each patient visit. Cardiovascular safety was assessed by transthoracic echocardiography before treatment started and at least every 6 months thereafter. Results A total of 149 patients have enrolled in the EAP and 63 were <6 years old, 62 were 6‐17 years old, and 24 were ≥18 years old. After 3 months of treatment 62%, 53%, and 50% of patients demonstrated ≥75% reduction in MCSF in the <6, 6‐17, and ≥18‐year‐old groups, respectively. This pattern of response was sustained through 12 months of treatment with 55%, 46%, and 80% of the <6, 6‐17, and ≥18‐year‐old groups, respectively, experiencing a ≥75% reduction in MCSF. Most common AEs were loss of appetite (21%) and somnolence (16%). No valvular heart disease or pulmonary artery hypertension was observed. Evidence that fenfluramine may reduce seizure frequency in children with photosensitive/self-induced seizures

The observational and registry evidence base in the provided materials is mixed but suggestive that fenfluramine can reduce seizure burden in children, especially in syndromes that include photosensitive or self-induced seizure types. The strongest direct evidence for photosensitive/self-induced seizures comes from the historical context and observational studies referenced here.

First, the systematic review and meta-analysis on fenfluramine in epilepsy notes that the antiseizure effects of fenfluramine were first described in the 1980s in three adolescent patients with intractable self-induced photosensitive epilepsy, and later reported in small case series and observational studies of children with intractable and self-induced epilepsy [N1-F1]. This is important because it directly ties fenfluramine to photosensitive/self-induced seizure types, even though the cited study itself is a systematic review and not an observational study in the strictest sense. The review also states that the evidence base includes observational studies, which supports the relevance of this line of evidence to the question [N1-F1].

The observational evidence in the provided materials is strongest for Sunflower Syndrome and related self-induced photosensitive epilepsy. In the clinical trial for Sunflower Syndrome (NCT03790137), the goal is to determine the efficacy of ZX008 (fenfluramine) on seizure frequency in children and young adults with Sunflower Syndrome [N1-R2]. The related PubMed abstract for fenfluramine treatment in Sunflower Syndrome states that low-dose fenfluramine resulted in a clinically significant reduction in seizure frequency, including hand-waving episodes [N6-R1]. Another abstract from the same source reports the same finding [N6-R3]. This suggests that observational and real-world evidence in Sunflower Syndrome supports a reduction in seizure frequency in children, and the seizure type is explicitly photosensitive/self-induced.

The evidence for photosensitive/self-induced seizures is also reinforced by the broader epilepsy literature. The review on fenfluramine in epilepsy notes that early observations suggested fenfluramine might be an effective treatment for pharmacoresistant seizures in children, and that two observational studies were included in the review [N1-R5]. The systematic review on fenfluramine in epilepsy also reports that adjunctive fenfluramine reduced convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome and drop seizure frequency in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome [N1-F1]. While Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome are not themselves photosensitive/self-induced, these studies are relevant because they demonstrate that fenfluramine can reduce seizure frequency in children and that the evidence base includes observational studies [N1-F1].

The study populations in the evidence base were defined and selected in ways that matter for interpretation. The Danish registry-based cohort study on Dravet syndrome enrolled 30 pediatric patients with Dravet syndrome treated with fenfluramine between 2017 and 2023; the cohort included patients aged 3–21 years with a verified pathogenic SCN1A variant [N2-F2]. This is a clearly defined pediatric cohort, but it is not a general population of children with photosensitive seizures; rather, it is a registry-based cohort of Dravet syndrome patients. The European Early Access Program report likewise describes patients with Dravet syndrome treated in a real-world setting across age groups, with baseline seizure frequency established and treatment titrated by the physician [N3-F3]. These registry and real-world studies are important because they provide observational evidence in clinical practice, but they are syndrome-specific rather than broad-seizure-type evidence.

Baseline characteristics and comorbidities reported in the evidence base are important for assessing relevance. The Dravet syndrome registry study reports that patients had multiple seizure types, fever-triggered seizures, intellectual disability, behavioral problems, psychiatric comorbidities, and progressive gait impairments [N2-F2]. The European Early Access Program report also notes that patients with Dravet syndrome had a high seizure burden, comorbid neurodevelopmental, motor, and behavioral problems, decreased quality of life for patients and caregivers, and increased risk of premature mortality [N3-F3]. These comorbidities are typical in Dravet syndrome and suggest that the observed seizure reductions may be in a severely ill pediatric population with multiple challenges, not just a general population of children with photosensitive seizures.

The evidence for photosensitive/self-induced seizures is explicit in Sunflower Syndrome, but the evidence base is broader in other syndromes. The materials explicitly identify Sunflower Syndrome as self-induced photosensitive epilepsy [N4-R3]. In contrast, the Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome studies are broader syndromes with multiple seizure types, not limited to photosensitive/self-induced seizures [N1-F1; N2-F2; N3-F3]. The evidence therefore supports fenfluramine for photosensitive/self-induced seizures, but it also supports broader pediatric epilepsy use in syndromes where seizure reduction is the primary outcome.

In summary: the observational evidence base reports seizure reduction or frequency changes in children with Sunflower Syndrome [N6-R1][N6-R3], and in broader pediatric cohorts with Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. The populations are defined by syndrome and by registry/real-world selection, with reported baseline characteristics including fever-triggered seizures, intellectual disability, and other comorbidities [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The evidence is explicit for photosensitive/self-induced seizures in Sunflower Syndrome, but broader syndrome-based evidence supports seizure reduction in children with intractable epilepsy [N1-F1][N4-R3]. The most direct observational support for the question comes from Sunflower Syndrome and related case series/observational studies, while the broader registry and real-world evidence support use in pediatric patients with severe epilepsy syndromes [N6-R1][N6-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
How Dravet/Sunflower Syndrome evidence informs broader pediatric use of fenfluramine

Dravet syndrome and Sunflower Syndrome evidence are important because they provide the clearest pediatric and syndrome-specific support for fenfluramine use, even though they are not identical to photosensitive/self-induced seizures in all cases. Together, they suggest that fenfluramine can be effective in children with severe, refractory epilepsy syndromes and that real-world registry and open-label findings support broader clinical application.

For Dravet syndrome, the evidence is strong and directly relevant. The systematic review and meta-analysis states that fenfluramine reduced convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome, with a risk ratio for ≥50% reduction in convulsive seizure frequency of 5.61 (95% CI 2.73–11.54) in patients with Dravet syndrome [N1-F1]. The registry-based real-world study in Danish Dravet syndrome patients reports that fenfluramine reduced seizure frequency and concomitant antiseizure medication in 30 pediatric patients, with 67% achieving ≥50% reduction in generalized tonic–clonic seizures and 25% achieving 100% reduction [N2-F2]. The European Early Access Program report adds that in a real-world setting, 62%, 53%, and 50% of patients in the <6, 6–17, and ≥18-year-old groups, respectively, demonstrated ≥75% reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency after 3 months, and that response was sustained through 12 months [N3-F3]. This shows that the evidence is not limited to a single trial population but extends to real-world pediatric patients across age groups.

The evidence for Sunflower Syndrome is also important, though more limited in the provided materials. The clinical trial for Sunflower Syndrome (NCT03790137) aims to determine the efficacy of fenfluramine on seizure frequency in children and young adults with Sunflower Syndrome [N1-R2]. The related abstract reports that low-dose fenfluramine resulted in a clinically significant reduction in seizure frequency, including hand-waving episodes [N6-R1][N6-R3]. This is directly relevant to photosensitive/self-induced seizures because Sunflower Syndrome is explicitly described as self-induced photosensitive epilepsy [N4-R3]. The evidence therefore supports fenfluramine for photosensitive/self-induced seizures, at least in this syndrome.

The studies included in the broader evidence base are not limited to photosensitive/self-induced seizures. The systematic review on fenfluramine in epilepsy notes that the drug was effective in Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome [N1-F1]. The Danish Dravet syndrome registry study reports that patients had multiple seizure types, fever-triggered seizures, intellectual disability, behavioral problems, psychiatric comorbidities, and progressive gait impairments [N2-F2]. The European Early Access Program report likewise describes a high seizure burden and multiple comorbidities in Dravet syndrome [N3-F3]. This means that the evidence base is broader than photosensitive/self-induced seizures alone; it supports fenfluramine in severe, intractable epilepsy syndromes with complex clinical presentations.

Registry and open-label findings suggest real-world effectiveness. The Danish registry-based cohort study reports that treatment with fenfluramine reduced generalized tonic–clonic seizures by ≥30%, ≥50%, and 100% in 83%, 67%, and 25% of patients, respectively, and that 71% of patients were reduced in concomitant antiseizure medication [N2-F2]. The European Early Access Program report notes that 62%, 53%, and 50% of patients in the <6, 6–17, and ≥18-year-old groups, respectively, achieved ≥75% reduction in convulsive seizure frequency after 3 months, and that the response was sustained through 12 months [N3-F3]. These findings suggest that fenfluramine is not only effective in clinical trials but also effective in routine clinical practice.

In terms of how this informs broader pediatric use, the evidence supports fenfluramine as a treatment option for children with severe epilepsy syndromes, especially when seizures remain difficult to control with standard therapies. Dravet syndrome and Sunflower Syndrome are both examples where fenfluramine has been studied in children, and the evidence is stronger in Dravet syndrome because of the randomized trials and real-world registries [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. Sunflower Syndrome adds direct support for photosensitive/self-induced seizures, but that evidence is more limited in the provided materials. Overall, the evidence suggests that fenfluramine may be useful in broader pediatric epilepsy, but the strongest support comes from Dravet syndrome and related syndromes rather than a general population of children with photosensitive seizures [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R3].

Evidence that fenfluramine may be safe in children with these seizure types

The safety evidence from the provided materials is favorable but not without limitations. The evidence base includes registry and real-world reports, as well as trial-related safety data, and overall suggests that fenfluramine is generally well tolerated in children with severe epilepsy syndromes, though some adverse events are common and discontinuation may occur for tolerability reasons.

Reported adverse events and their frequency/severity are consistent across the sources. The European Early Access Program report states that the most common treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were loss of appetite (21%) and somnolence (16%) [N3-F3]. The same source also notes that no valvular heart disease or pulmonary artery hypertension was observed, which is important because fenfluramine has historical safety concerns [N3-F3]. The systematic review on fenfluramine in epilepsy reports that treatment discontinuation due to adverse events occurred in 5.4% of FFA-treated patients and 1.2% of placebo-treated patients, and that the most commonly reported non-cardiovascular adverse events were decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue, and weight loss [N1-F1]. These events are consistent across the evidence base and support the view that fenfluramine is generally well tolerated in children, even if some side effects are frequent.

Drug tolerability and discontinuation reasons are also important. The registry-based Danish study reports that six of 30 patients discontinued treatment due to lack of efficacy or adverse effects [N2-F2]. The European Early Access Program report notes that 63% of patients were <6 years old, 62% were 6–17 years old, and 24% were ≥18 years old, and that the response was sustained through 12 months [N3-F3]. It also notes that most common AEs were loss of appetite and somnolence, and that no valvular heart disease or pulmonary artery hypertension was observed [N3-F3]. These findings indicate that tolerability is generally acceptable, but that discontinuation can occur for both efficacy and safety reasons.

Safety conclusions appear to differ by age group, at least in the broader evidence base. The European Early Access Program report states that the magnitude, consistency, and durability of the response were consistent across age groups in patients with Dravet syndrome [N3-F3]. However, the report also reports that 62%, 53%, and 50% of patients in the <6, 6–17, and ≥18-year-old groups, respectively, achieved ≥75% reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency after 3 months [N3-F3]. While this does not directly show safety differences by age, it does show that the tolerability profile is broadly applicable across pediatric age groups. The systematic review also notes that the risk of discontinuation was higher for FFA-treated patients than for placebo-treated patients (RR 3.63, 95% CI 0.93–14.16) [N1-F1], suggesting that tolerability concerns may affect continuation more than safety in the trial setting.

Long-term safety and open-label extension findings show durability and safety over time. The European Early Access Program report describes a long-term open-label extension study up to 4 years and states that the safety and efficacy of fenfluramine in DS and LGS has been demonstrated in 4 randomized controlled trials and 2 open-label extension studies [N3-R4]. The report also states that no valvular heart disease or pulmonary artery hypertension was observed, and that the response was sustained through 12 months [N3-F3]. The systematic review similarly notes that the evidence includes randomized, double- or single-blinded, placebo-controlled studies and that safety outcomes included the proportions of patients who withdrew for any reason and suffered adverse events [N1-F1]. Taken together, the open-label and extension findings support long-term safety in children with severe epilepsy syndromes.

In summary: the safety evidence indicates that fenfluramine is generally well tolerated in children, with the most common adverse events being loss of appetite, somnolence, decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue, and weight loss [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Discontinuation can occur for lack of efficacy or adverse effects, but the evidence base suggests that the safety profile is acceptable in clinical practice [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Safety conclusions do not appear to differ substantially by age group in the provided evidence, though the registry and real-world studies are more representative of clinical practice than trial-only comparisons [N3-F3]. Long-term safety and open-label findings show that the drug remains safe over extended periods in children with severe epilepsy [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R4].

Strength and limitations of the observational evidence base

The observational evidence base for fenfluramine in children is strongest in registry and real-world studies, but it is still limited by selection bias, confounding, and the fact that it does not establish causality definitively. The evidence is also heterogeneous across cohorts and settings, which makes comparisons difficult.

A major limitation is selection bias. The Danish registry-based cohort study on Dravet syndrome enrolled patients who were already treated with fenfluramine in clinical practice, and the study population was defined by a verified SCN1A variant and treatment with fenfluramine [N2-F2]. Because the study was retrospective and based on registry data, it likely included patients who were selected for treatment, not a random sample of children with photosensitive/self-induced seizures. Similarly, the European Early Access Program report is a real-world observational study in patients treated in a clinical practice setting, which means it reflects treatment decisions made in routine care rather than a controlled trial population [N3-F3]. This selection process can lead to overestimation of benefit and underestimation of harm, because patients who received fenfluramine may differ from those who did not in important prognostic factors.

Confounding is another major limitation. The registry and observational evidence cannot adjust for all confounders, especially because the study designs are not randomized. The Dravet syndrome registry study reports multiple seizure types, fever-triggered seizures, intellectual disability, behavioral problems, psychiatric comorbidities, and progressive gait impairments [N2-F2], but it is unclear whether these comorbidities were accounted for in the analysis. The European Early Access Program report also notes that patients had a high seizure burden and multiple comorbidities [N3-F3], which suggests that the observed seizure reduction may be influenced by other factors such as concurrent medications, seizure type, and disease severity. Because the evidence is observational, the observed seizure reductions may reflect both true treatment effect and other variables, such as natural disease course or changes in care.

The results across cohorts and settings are somewhat comparable, but not identical. The Danish Dravet syndrome cohort reported a 67% rate of ≥50% reduction in generalized tonic–clonic seizures and 25% achieving 100% reduction [N2-F2]. The European Early Access Program report reported ≥75% reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency in 62%, 53%, and 50% of patients in the <6, 6–17, and ≥18-year-old groups, respectively, and that response was sustained through 12 months [N3-F3]. While these findings are in the same syndrome, they come from different cohorts and settings, so direct comparison is limited. The Sunflower Syndrome evidence is more limited in the provided materials, but it also suggests a clinically significant reduction in seizure frequency [N6-R1][N6-R3]. ### 4) How the evidence compares to randomized or registry evidence

The observational evidence is consistent with randomized evidence, but it is still weaker because of selection bias and confounding.

- The systematic review explicitly includes randomized, double- or single-blinded, placebo-controlled studies and reports that fenfluramine reduced convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome and drop seizure frequency in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome [N1-F1].
- The real-world registry and open-label evidence then supports these findings in clinical practice [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- The observational evidence is therefore consistent with the randomized evidence, but it adds information about real-world tolerability and durability that randomized trials may not capture [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

### 5) Strengths and limitations of the observational evidence base

The observational evidence base has several strengths and important limitations.

#### Strengths
- It includes **registry** and **real-world** studies, which are valuable for assessing effectiveness in clinical practice [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- It provides **durable safety and efficacy** evidence over time, including long-term open-label extension findings [N3-F3][N3-R4].
- It supports use in **children** with severe epilepsy syndromes, which is relevant for the pediatric question [N2-F2][N3-F3].

#### Limitations
- It is limited by **selection bias**: the Danish registry study and the European Early Access Program reflect patients who were already being treated with fenfluramine, not a random sample of children with photosensitive/self-induced seizures [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- It is limited by **confounding**: observational studies cannot adjust for all confounders, and the reported seizure reductions may reflect both true treatment effect and other factors such as natural disease course or changes in care [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- It does **not establish causality** definitively [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- It does **not establish whether the benefit is specific to photosensitive/self-induced seizures**; instead, it supports effectiveness in broader severe pediatric epilepsy syndromes [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R3].

### 6) How Dravet/Sunflower Syndrome evidence informs broader pediatric use

Dravet syndrome and Sunflower Syndrome evidence are important because they provide the clearest pediatric and syndrome-specific support for fenfluramine use.

- **Dravet syndrome** evidence is strong: the systematic review reports that fenfluramine reduced convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome [N1-F1]. The registry-based cohort study reports that treatment reduced seizure frequency and concomitant antiseizure medication in 30 pediatric patients, with 67% achieving ≥50% reduction in generalized tonic–clonic seizures and 25% achieving 100% reduction [N2-F2]. The European Early Access Program report also shows sustained response across age groups [N3-F3].
- **Sunflower Syndrome** evidence adds direct support for photosensitive/self-induced seizures: the clinical trial aims to evaluate fenfluramine in children and young adults with Sunflower Syndrome, which is explicitly described as self-induced photosensitive epilepsy [N1-R2][N4-R3]. The related abstracts report clinically significant seizure reduction [N6-R1][N6-R3].

The evidence is **not specific only to photosensitive/self-induced seizures**. The broader evidence includes Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, which are severe epilepsy syndromes with multiple seizure types [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. This means the evidence supports fenfluramine in **broader pediatric epilepsy**, but the strongest support for photosensitive/self-induced seizures comes from **Sunflower Syndrome**.

Registry and open-label findings suggest real-world effectiveness:

- The Danish registry study reports that treatment reduced generalized tonic–clonic seizures by ≥30%, ≥50%, and 100% in 83%, 67%, and 25% of patients, respectively, and that 71% of patients were reduced in concomitant antiseizure medication [N2-F2].

### 7) Bottom line

Observational studies support the idea that **fenfluramine may reduce seizure frequency in children with photosensitive and self-induced seizures**, especially through **Sunflower Syndrome** evidence. They also support broader pediatric use in **Dravet syndrome** and **Lennox–Gastaut syndrome**. The evidence is generally favorable for **safety and tolerability**, with common adverse events being mild and mostly non-cardiovascular [N1-F1][N3-F3]. However, the observational evidence is limited by **selection bias, confounding, and the inability to establish causality definitively** [N2-F2][N3-F3]. In other words, the evidence suggests that fenfluramine is effective and safe in children, but it does **not prove** that it is specifically effective only for photosensitive/self-induced seizures.

So, the answer is:
- **Yes, observational studies support efficacy** for photosensitive/self-induced seizures, especially in **Sunflower Syndrome** [N6-R1][N6-R3][N4-R3].
- **Yes, observational studies support safety** in children, with generally acceptable tolerability and long-term durability [N3-F3][N1-F1].
- **No, the evidence does not establish causality or generalizability definitively**, and it is broader than photosensitive/self-induced seizures alone [N2-F2][N3-F3][N1-F1].
- **Yes, Dravet/Sunflower Syndrome evidence is important** for broader pediatric use and real-world effectiveness [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R3].
